extracted.intended_audience: gentlemen seeking service at court / courtiers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the behaviour, dress, conversation, friendship, obedience, and reputation management expected of a courtier serving princes and moving in noble society. Focuses on practical rules of modesty, adaptation to customs, balancing duty and initiative, and cultivating honourable reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier should be modest (not presumptuous) and combine modesty with worth; modesty greatly honours its possessor when united with high worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modesty must not be so excessive as to become timid or proud; avoid being 'so reserved that they shun human company beyond reason.' Be fluent on occasion, prudent and sagacious in discussing statecraft, adapt to local customs, be agreeable about lesser matters, and above all 'make for right; not envious, not evil-tongued.' Do not seek favour by 'foul ways or dishonourable means.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to customs and company
rubrics_metrics.description: A Courtier should have the good sense to adapt himself to the customs of the nations where he finds himself and govern himself according to the character of the prince he serves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe the character of your master: if the prince is severe, follow orders to the letter. In conversation, adapt topics (grave matters, festivals, games) to the quality of the company; vary conversation to avoid tedious repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience vs. initiative (weighing disobedience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not deviate from a superior's commands lightly; if considering departure from orders, weigh the probable gain of success against the greater harm of failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the damage from failure exceeds the gain from success, carry out orders strictly; if the possible gain outweighs the potential damage, one may properly venture to follow one's reason ('act like good merchants, who to gain much risk little, but never risk much to gain little'). Beware starting a fashion of rating commands lightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of obedience in dishonourable acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A gentleman is not bound to obey any man in dishonourable things; one must refuse commands that bring injury or disgrace to the lord or are acts of treachery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Messer Federico asserts one is bound not to commit treachery; note the text's caveat that some things which appear evil may in context be permissible — distinguishing the truly good from what only seems so is necessary (the page defers full treatment to the reader's wisdom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaving a vicious master
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Courtier finds himself in the service of a vicious or malign master, he should depart as soon as he discovers it, except that duty to remain in war or adversity may justify staying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duty ought to outweigh other reasons; do not desert a patron in adversity (lest thought to have left for gain), but at other times it is right to leave service likely to disgrace the gentleman before good men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress and outward appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: A Courtier should generally follow the custom of the majority, be neat and dainty, and display modest elegance rather than extremes of fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extreme amplitude or scantiness; prefer sober colours (black or somewhat dark) for ordinary attire, reserve showy/gaily coloured garments for armour or public festivals. Do not obsess over one detail (hair, teeth, beard, boots) to the neglect of overall neatness. Dress to aid how you wish to be regarded, since 'things external often bear witness to the things within.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding foolish ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not adopt silly, overly-decorated fashions that mark a man as a fool or buffoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quartered garments in diverse colours, masses of strings, knotted ribbons, cross lacings — such trappings cause onlookers to take a man for a fool. Nevertheless, if a fashion is universal in a place it becomes less a personal fault; still, the Courtier should aim for modest elegance rather than borrowed or tasteless details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using outward manner as signal (appearance and gestures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outward ways — walking, laughing, looking, gestures — often give knowledge of the inner qualities of a man and serve as indicators of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that posture, carriage, and habitual looks may cause instant judgments (e.g., a certain twist of the head or silly laugh marks someone as frivolous). These non-verbal signs inform others even before words or acts are known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct in conversation and amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier should be able to vary his conversation, adapt to company, be affable and not babble merely to be seen in favour; play amusements in moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cling to the well-dressed merely to be seen; avoid babbling to show importance. Games (cards, dice, chess, other amusements) are acceptable unless engaged in constantly to the neglect of important matters, or played solely to win money or display avarice. Games should not substitute for learning a noble science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivating and managing friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose intimate friends carefully—consort with the good, wise, discreet; friendship greatly affects reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer friends of like mind; have if possible one special hearty friend, and otherwise love, honour and respect others according to their worth. Be courteous, kind, generous, affable, mild, zealous to serve friends' welfare, endure natural defects, correct kindly, and avoid thrusting oneself forward or being unseasonably contentious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation management and the use of fame
rubrics_metrics.description: Where unknown, see that a good opinion of you precedes you; reputation prepared by many judgments makes later acceptance easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate fame among other lords, ladies and gentlemen so that good opinion will predispose people to admire you; but beware over-inflated report — reports may lead to disappointment when the eye judges immediately. Men's characters are less visible at first than objects, so reputation tends to be confirmed by ongoing acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive trust and realistic prudence in friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: While perfect friendship is highly valued, do not trust blindly; be aware that even long friendships may end in deceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reveal all thoughts to any friend as to yourself; love and serve by merit but be prudent. The Courtier should avoid giving himself up entirely to friendship that can later bring betrayal; retain discretion while seeking steadfast companionship.
